Therefore I say that my hon. friends immediately opposite, who are now crying similar blue ruin with respect to the temporary wheat surplus, may be just as incorrect as they were in the previous two years, and as the Tories were a year ago in regard to unemployment. In any event, I have listened

The Address-Mr. Philpott very carefully for ten full days to the speeches made by hon. gentlemen of the opposition, and with one exception I have yet to hear from the Tory benches, the C.C.F. benches, or the Social Credit benches one single suggestion to the government of Canada or the wheat board of Canada as to how they can sell one single extra bushel of wheat, or for that m^fter how they can even give away a single bushel of wheat, because no practical suggestion has been made except by one hon. gentleman, namely the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) who did make a practical proposition.
We have heard the question from the opposition benches, can the leopard change its spots? I submit that the Tory leopard has not changed its spots, because the only election they really won in this whole century on their own merits was the election of 1911, and they won it on the cry of "no truck or trade with the Yankees".
I sat back in this debate to the very end, hoping that the Tories would repent at last of the atrocious statement of policy which was made in this house two years ago by their official spokesman on international affairs, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who laid down in most explicit terms the proposition that we should mot sell a single bushel of wheat or a single pound of butter to any part of the communist world, which is one-third of the world. So far as we have been able to hear, not a single member of the Tory opposition has risen in his place and suggested that this policy should be reversed. If I am wrong I hope they will correct me later on in the debate on international affairs.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when I say there has been no new idea put out by the Tory party in this century except the Bennett buggy, it seems to me I am on solid ground because, whereas in 1911 it was "no truck or trade with the Yankees", in the year 1956, and in the election of 1957 or 1958, obviously the Tory cry is going to be "no truck or trade with the communists"-one-third of the world

"no truck or trade with China, Russia, or the 100 million in the satellite countries who are held in servitude".
I say, Mr. Speaker, nothing has emerged :in this debate, or anywhere else I have seen, to suggest that there is to be any change in the next election. Today the hon. member for Broadview talked about the Gallup poll. Well, it seems to me that just as in the last election when they galloped to their doom on the phony issue of horses on the payroll, today they are nosediving to disaster on the

equally phony issue of the 15 unarmed Harvard trainers that Egypt is trying to buy.
If this government has and retains the confidence of the people of Canada and the respect of the people of the world, it is due to a very simple fact, namely that the Liberals are a peacemaker party, and our government has respect all over the world as one of the great, practical, peacemaking aggregations in the world today.
Let us look at what happened in the past year. We had no fewer than three cabinet ministers abroad on peacemaking missions. We had the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) in his own way doing a very fine job and, as it turned out, at considerable physical cost to himself. We had our past master peacemaker, the veteran Secretary of State for External Affairs who, for my money, is the most practical peacemaker in the whole world today. If it is true-and it is true-that we won a tremendous success at the United Nations in that so-called package deal, it was not entirely owing to the man to whom I intend to come in a moment. It was owing to the fact that for many, many years the Secretary of State for External Affairs had carefully laid the groundwork for the great success the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) was finally able to bring about at Lake Success.
It seems to me that if the Minister of National Health and Welfare was able to obtain that tremendous victory at New York it was for two reasons. The first apparently is because he is also a practical peacemaker well worthy to sit beside the Secretary of State for External Affairs. But it was also because the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his own person represented what is the great opportunity of our time. He is both the man trying to make peace at New York and the man in charge of social welfare in Canada. When he struggled with all his might and with such great skill to get those 16 nations into the United Nations, I believe that what he was really thinking was this. If we can get peace in the world we can have in Canada higher old age pensions, better family allowances and, at the right time, health insurance; we can do all the things that have to be done when we get the full welfare state instead of the warfare state. But you cannot get the welfare state instead of the warfare state until you get real peace. The package deal was a great contribution to that state of peace.
I do not intend to try to keep the house beyond the time limit, but I will say this. I do not know at what time the people of

Canada will decide it is time for a change and time once again to try the same old Tory party with the same old Bennett buggies that we had in the thirties. If they so decide, it is all right with me. In the present Leader of the Opposition I think they will get as good a Tory prime minister as there has ever been since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald; but for my money I hope the people of Canada will allow the present prime minister, who is approaching his 74th birthday, to serve quite as long as did that grand old British oak, that great statesman Sir Winston Churchill, who served to the full age of 81.
I remember how well and how often my Tory friends on the other side of the chamber-including, I believe, my good and second oldest personal friend in the house, the Leader of the Opposition-applauded the fact that the great leader of the British Conservative party was able to serve to the grand and ripe age of 81. Perhaps in God's good grace and with the consent of the Canadian people a Liberal prime minister of Canada may serve to the great age attained by Gladstone, that grand old Liberal of Britain who served, I believe, until he was no less than 84.
We talk about the grand old British oak. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is about our hard Canadian maple one thing which makes it well worthy to stand beside that grand old British oak. The Canadian maple is never so glorious as it is in the autumn. Who knows but that in God's good grace the most glorious years of achievement of the present Prime Minister of Canada may be in the future seven years which would give him a service record equal in length to that of the grand old man of British politics.

speechtext:
1.	Have steps been taken since the end of the last session to provide unemployment insurance coverage for Canadians employed by the United States government and its agencies on Newfoundland bases?
2.	If so, what are they and what coverage is now in effect?
3.	If not, what steps are being taken to provide for such coverage?

subtopic: CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer I shall give will apply to all three parts of question No. 4.
Negotiations have been initiated with the United States government and are continuing in the matter of providing unemployment insurance coverage for Canadian civilians employed in Canada by the armed forces of the United States. That, of course, includes the area mentioned in the question.
There are indications that a satisfactory solution of this problem will result from these negotiations. I hope to be in a position to make a more positive statement on this subject at a later date during this session.
What progress has been made, since the last session of parliament, to bring into effect unemployment insurance for fishermen in British Columbia?

Mr. Speaker, I was notified on the orders of the day of a question from the bon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) in almost the same terms as this question. My reply, of course, shall apply not only to British Columbia but to the east and west coasts as well as to inland waters.
Hon. members will recall that this question was discussed at some length in the standing committee on industrial relations last session. Much of this discussion will be found from page 299 to page 326 of the minutes of proceedings of that committee. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and officials of his department appeared before the committee. During those discussions I think most of those participating reluctantly had to agree that it would be difficult to bring under the Unemployment Insurance Act those who are owners or are self-employed or who fish on a straight share basis. In view of this, it was felt that even if the remainder-approximately 7 per cent-who go out to fish, namely the wage earners, could be brought under the act and have their fishing employment count along with other employment toward benefits it would be unfair to the main body of the fishermen.
Consequently there was brought about something of a reorientation of the studies related to the whole fisherman group, whereby the Department of Fisheries undertook to explore every possible means of better stabilization of revenue on behalf of the self-employed and those on a share basis, and co-ordinated with that effort the unemployment insurance commission would make further efforts toward fitting the remainder, namely the wage earners, under the insurance plan.
I should add that during the past summer a senior officer of the commission made a firsthand investigation of the practices followed in the United Kingdom and in several European countries where fishing is an important industry. The commission's report on this investigation has not yet been received, but when it is it will be turned over for study.
